    Getting Started

    getting-started.Rmd
    library(xtrial)

    Let’s start with a simple example: a cross-trial causal comparison problem where we want to estimate the effect of treatment a versus treatment b when the two randomized trials do not share the same active comparator.

    The xtrial package provides a common interface for fitting several estimators under different identification strategies. These include:

    • inverse probability weighting (IPW),
    • g-computation,
    • one-step / efficient influence function (EIF) estimation, and
    • targeted minimum loss-based estimation (TMLE).

    The package also supports several comparison strategies, including traditional indirect comparison, observational comparison, direct pooled IPD comparison, and indirect pooled IPD comparison.

    Simulating Example Data

    For illustration, we will use a simulated dataset generated by simulate_xtrial_data(). The data-generating mechanism is motivated by cross-trial tuberculosis treatment comparisons.

    dat <- simulate_xtrial_data(
  n = 1000
)

head(dat)
#>   s         L1 L2 country treatment y
#> 1 1 -0.7115241  0       2         a 0
#> 2 1  0.6621788  0       1       sc2 0
#> 3 2 -0.7088698  1       4       sc1 0
#> 4 1  0.1979580  1       4         a 0
#> 5 1 -1.2035661  0       3         a 0
#> 6 2 -1.0398170  0       3       sc1 0

    The simulated data contain the outcome, treatment assignment, study indicator, and baseline covariates needed by the estimators in xtrial.

    A First Analysis

    The main user-facing function is xtrial(). A simple call fits one comparison approach with one estimator.

    For example, the following code fits a TMLE estimator using the direct pooled IPD comparison approach.

    fit <- xtrial(
  data = dat,
  approach = "direct",
  estimator = "tmle",
  nuisance_type = "simple"
)

fit
#> 
#> xtrial object
#> 
#> Estimator: TMLE 
#> Approach : Direct 
#> 
#> Estimate : 0.0140
#> SE       : 0.0488
#> 
#> 95% CI:
#> (-0.0816, 0.1097)

    Notice what xtrial() returns: an object containing the point estimate, standard error, confidence interval, and information about the fitted approach and estimator.

    We can store the fitted object and summarize it:

    summary(fit)
#>   estimator approach   estimate         se      ci_low  ci_high
#> 1      tmle   direct 0.01400569 0.04879952 -0.08163961 0.109651

    Reusing Arguments

    When fitting several estimators to the same dataset, it is often helpful to store repeated arguments first. This keeps the calls short and makes the analysis easier to read.

    comparison_data <- dat
comparison_approach <- "direct"

fit_tmle <- xtrial(
  data = comparison_data,
  approach = comparison_approach,
  estimator = "tmle",
  nuisance_type = "simple"
)

fit_tmle
#> 
#> xtrial object
#> 
#> Estimator: TMLE 
#> Approach : Direct 
#> 
#> Estimate : 0.0140
#> SE       : 0.0488
#> 
#> 95% CI:
#> (-0.0816, 0.1097)

    Trying Different Estimators

    We can compare several estimators under the same identification strategy.

    fit_ipw <- xtrial(
  data = comparison_data,
  approach = comparison_approach,
  estimator = "ipw",
  nuisance_type = "simple"
)

fit_gcomp <- xtrial(
  data = comparison_data,
  approach = comparison_approach,
  estimator = "gcomp",
  nuisance_type = "simple"
)

fit_onestep <- xtrial(
  data = comparison_data,
  approach = comparison_approach,
  estimator = "onestep",
  nuisance_type = "simple"
)

fit_tmle <- xtrial(
  data = comparison_data,
  approach = comparison_approach,
  estimator = "tmle",
  nuisance_type = "simple"
)

    The fitted objects can then be printed or summarized individually.

    fit_ipw

#> (-0.1021, 0.1765)

fit_onestep

    Trying Different Comparison Approaches

    The same estimator can also be used with different comparison approaches.

    fit_traditional <- xtrial(
  data = comparison_data,
  approach = "traditional",
  estimator = "tmle",
  nuisance_type = "simple"
)

fit_observational <- xtrial(
  data = comparison_data,
  approach = "observational",
  estimator = "tmle",
  nuisance_type = "simple"
)

fit_direct <- xtrial(
  data = comparison_data,
  approach = "direct",
  estimator = "tmle",
  nuisance_type = "simple"
)

fit_indirect <- xtrial(
  data = comparison_data,
  approach = "indirect",
  estimator = "tmle",
  nuisance_type = "simple"
)
    fit_traditional

    Simple and Flexible Nuisance Estimation

    Some estimators require nuisance functions, such as outcome regressions, treatment mechanisms, or study membership probabilities. The argument nuisance_type controls how these nuisance functions are estimated.

    For a fast, reproducible example, we use nuisance_type = "simple" above. When flexible estimation is desired, use:

    fit_flexible <- xtrial(
  data = comparison_data,
  approach = "direct",
  estimator = "tmle",
  nuisance_type = "flexible"
)

fit_flexible

    Flexible nuisance estimation may be slower, but it can be useful when the working models used by the simple implementation are too restrictive.

    A Minimal Workflow

    A typical xtrial workflow is:

    1. prepare or simulate a dataset with the required outcome, treatment, study, and covariate variables;
    2. choose an identification approach;
    3. choose an estimator;
    4. call xtrial(); and
    5. inspect the estimate, standard error, and confidence interval.

    For example:

    dat <- simulate_xtrial_data(n = 1000)

fit <- xtrial(
  data = dat,
  approach = "direct",
  estimator = "tmle",
  nuisance_type = "simple"
)

summary(fit)
#>   estimator approach   estimate         se      ci_low   ci_high
#> 1      tmle   direct 0.07424915 0.04894494 -0.02168118 0.1701795
